Issued at 126 PM CDT Fri Sep 11 2026

Despite being a tad on the breezy side, its turning out to be a
nice albeit warm September afternoon. Current temps range in 
the 80s and are forecast to reach the upper 80s across western 
MN this afternoon where warm advection is currently strongest. 
Wind gusts continue to peak between 30-40 mph along the Buffalo 
Ridge whereas most other sites report gusts between 20-30 mph 
this afternoon. Winds are expected to decrease late tonight into
early tomorrow once a cold front tracks through the northern 
plains later this evening. Latest water vapor imagery shows a 
deepening ridge extending north and east of the Great Lakes 
region while an elongated troughing pattern stretches from the 
northern plains over the PacNorthwest. Embedded within this 
troughing pattern is a low-level wave which will serve as our 
next feature of interest over the next 12-24 hours. Skies this 
afternoon our ahead of the wave will gradually increase from 
west for the remainder of the evening.

Current mesoanalysis features an h85 low located over central 
South Dakota. Ahead of this low, a strong 40-50kt LLJ is 
transporting warmer and moist air up into the northern plains. 
Additionally, a SW to NW oriented swath of mixed layer 
instability of ~1000 J/kg exists which has allowed for continued
isolated convective pulses on radar. Luckily, enough inhibition
is in place to keep any precip development isolated and brief. 
However, that will not be the case as head into later this 
afternoon and evening. The aforementioned h85 low will continue 
to track east into MN through the rest of today. As this occurs,
low-level forcing becomes maximized while CINH erodes, and 
lapse rates deepen to 7.0 to 7.5 deg C/km. This environment will
allow for better organized convection to initiate over west- 
central and northern MN. Since early this morning, the SPC has 
reduced the Slight Risk (level 2 of 5) spatially to be confined 
more to central and northern Minnesota this evening. Forecast 
guidance continues to advertise much of the strongest convection
mainly north of a line that extends from Morris to St. Cloud. 
Early in the event, forecast hodographs advertise sufficient 
effective- layer shear combined with low LCLs nearing 1km. Thus 
any supercells that manage to get their act together could be 
conducive enough to support a tornado or two and large hail. As 
the line continues east into central and eastern MN this 
evening, the line transitions into more a of damaging wind gust 
threat. By tonight, the wave driving these storms reaches 
western WI. Although forcing will not be as strong as previous 
hours, rain showers and sub-severe storms are expected to 
develop along the axis of residual instability. Total QPF will 
vary depending on where the strongest rainfall occurs this 
evening but areas north and west of a line from Mora down to 
Appleton could see a couple hundredths to a quarter of an inch 
of rain with higher localized amounts. Areas across western 
Wisconsin could see a hundredth or tenth of an inch.

Most of the weekend appears fairly tranquil. Winds will remain a 
tad breezy out of the NW on Saturday morning near 20kts but 
will decrease as surface high pressure becomes the dominant 
feature through the daylight hours. Skies during this time 
should remain mostly clear. By Saturday night, a narrow band of 
forcing will move across southern MN that is part of upper-level
troughing over Hudson Bay area. Scattered rain showers could 
develop mostly across southern Minnesota during this time but 
the majority of Sunday features partly cloudy to mostly clear 
skies by the afternoon. Its isn't until Monday that we see the 
arrival of our next widespread rainfall chances. A stacked 998mb
low will sweep across the International Border. Widespread 
rainfall will move from west to east throughout much of the day.
Most precip looks in the form of rain and some embedded thunder
however, areas along and south of the I-90 corridor could see a
stronger storm or two Monday evening. QPF for this episode 
continue to trend downward. The NBM and EPS have favored 
widespread 1-2" rain totals but the more realistic solutions 
appear with the GEFS. Thus have shifted the 1-2" swath farther 
south and east in southern MN into western WI. Areas north of 
this region would more so observe a half inch to closer to an 
inch. 

If you're a lover of "sweater weather" or enjoy a cup of hot apple 
cider then the temperature forecast will make you happy. Saturday 
begins our downward temp trend. Forecast highs will only warm into 
the low to mid-70s and then even cooler on Sunday in the upper 60s, 
with lows in the mid to upper 40s. But wait there's more! This 
cooler airmass should hang around through much of next week 
with highs mainly in the upper 60s and lows near 50.
